name: Plant Respiration
author: @praisejamesx
tagline: Watch the plant, not just the number.
summary: A one-plant change monitor. It compares the host's baseline-relative response to each channel's measured noise, withholds the call when the enclosure moved, and keeps a session history for a same-time-of-day comparison.
scope: Decide whether one plant's mixed-gas response on one array has moved beyond that array's own noise on this window, and keep the care context needed to interpret a change. It supports inspection; it does not identify a compound, a pest, a pathogen, or a care fault.
limits: Same plant, same array, same enclosure, and the same time of day. A reading does not transfer across arrays, rooms, or seasons.
The response is a mixed gas signal. Water, light, temperature, humidity, handling, cleaning products, people, and sensor drift all move it.
No ethylene, CO₂, or compound channel. No pest, pathogen, or deficiency identification.
A quiet array does not clear a plant with visible symptoms, and a change is not a diagnosis.
whatItIs: A structured log for one plant. It helps you notice a VOC or respiration change and correlate it with care, light, and visible symptoms.
whatItIsNot: Not ethylene detection, not a pest or pathogen diagnosis, not a substitute for inspecting roots and leaves, and not a cross-rig claim.
citations: Kesselmeier, J. & Staudt, M. (1999). Biogenic volatile organic compounds (VOC): an overview. Journal of Atmospheric Chemistry 33, 23–88.
Dicke, M. & Baldwin, I. T. (2010). The evolutionary context for herbivore-induced plant volatiles: beyond the ‘cry for help’. Trends in Plant Science 15(3), 167–175.
Matsui, K. (2006). Green leaf volatiles: hydroperoxide lyase pathway of oxylipin metabolism. Current Opinion in Plant Biology 9(4), 409–415.
Caird, M. A., Richards, J. H. & Donovan, L. A. (2007). Nighttime stomatal conductance and transpiration in C3 and C4 plants. Plant Physiology 143(1), 4–10.

Barsan, N. & Weimar, U. (2003). Understanding the fundamental principles of metal oxide based gas sensors; the example of CO sensing with SnO2 sensors in the presence of humidity. Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter 15(20), R813–R839.

widgets.title: Plant Respiration
widgets.subtitle: One plant, one array. A change beyond noise, with the care context attached.
widgets.note: Example Vial · sandboxed UI · profile-declared detector

widgets.headline: A change signal is not a diagnosis.
widgets.body: The array can notice that one plant’s volatile profile changed on this array. It cannot tell you why. Check water, light, pests, roots, and recent moves.
always: Record light, watering, and leaf condition with every sample.
Inspect the roots and the undersides of leaves before changing care.
Compare at the same time of day and re-baseline after a move.
never: Never treat a sensor change as a pest or disease identification.
Never assume the array can see ethylene; there is no ethylene channel.
Never compare a plant’s reading to a different array or rig.

widgets.title: What this workspace is allowed to claim

items.label: Array can do
items.hint: Same plant, same array, same time of day, against that channel’s own noise.

items.label: Array cannot do
items.hint: No ethylene channel and no pest, pathogen, or care-fault identification.

items.label: Best signal
items.hint: A change that holds for most of the window, seen at the same time of day across sessions.

widgets.title: The plant, as a checklist
widgets.caption: Click a point. The sensor is one clue; the plant body is the rest of the evidence.

hotspots.label: Leaf surface
hotspots.body: Look for spots, curling, yellowing, sticky honeydew, webbing, or a change in leaf gloss. Check the underside, not just the top.

hotspots.label: Stem
hotspots.body: Soft, black, or constricted stems are structural problems the array cannot name. Record them with the reading.

hotspots.label: Soil / pot
hotspots.body: Overwatering and poor drainage can look like a slow decline. Smell the soil, check moisture, and look for fungus gnats.

hotspots.label: Roots
hotspots.body: Root rot can be invisible above the pot. If the plant is declining without an obvious leaf cause, inspect the root ball.

hotspots.label: Sensor
hotspots.body: Same array, same distance, same time of day. Temperature and humidity are confounds; log them. The array sees a VOC mixture, not ethylene.

steps.label: Baseline
steps.body: Pick one plant and one location. Record light, watering, pot size, and leaf condition. Let the host form a ready baseline on this array.

steps.label: Weekly
steps.body: Sample at the same time of day. Save a session with the change index and enclosure readings, then log water, light, and leaf notes.

steps.label: Change
steps.body: A sustained change is a prompt to inspect. Look for pests, root problems, drafts, or a recent move before changing care.

steps.label: Review
steps.body: Compare the session trend, not one point. Re-baseline after a move, repot, or season change.

widgets.title: What to do with a change

rules.then: Check water, heat, and root health. Isolate if pests are visible. Do not treat the number as the cause.

rules.when: Sustained rise plus sticky leaves or webbing
rules.then: Inspect for pests, especially under the leaves. Do not spray blindly.
Look at roots, drainage, and light. The array may be blind to the cause.
Re-baseline after the move. Do not compare readings across rooms or seasons.
Do not use smell as exposure measurement. Ventilate and seek appropriate guidance.

items.label: Roots / drainage checked

widgets.title: Use this with your rig
widgets.body: Let the host form a ready baseline on the same array, at the same distance, with the enclosure closed. Save a session at the same time of day. The workspace withholds the change call while the baseline is warming or the enclosure moved.

docs.title: How the change call is made
body: The host applies the profile’s baseline and response transform. The workspace reads the baseline-relative response (value minus R0, over R0) from the host and never recomputes a hidden baseline of its own.

The Vial’s declared profile is the detector. The host requires at least two channels to clear their sensitivity-scaled budget on the same sample, applies the profile’s 90 s warning persistence and 25% hysteresis, and refuses to arm when the baseline is not ready or channel coverage is below 80%. The profile’s 0.6 confidence floor also applies to the final call.

The workspace’s twice-CV band is an explanation of channel noise, not a second detector. A response outside that band is shown as an excursion; it becomes a change call only when the profile detector confirms a sustained change.

If temperature moved 1.5 °C or more, or humidity moved 5 %RH or more, during the window, the change call is withheld. A MOX response is temperature- and humidity-sensitive, so the change cannot be attributed to the plant.

docs.title: The measurement protocol
body: One plant, one location, one enclosure, one array. Keep the distance and the sampling time the same; stomatal state follows the light cycle, so a different clock time is a different measurement.
Let the array equilibrate. The profile waits 180 s before it trusts a baseline and uses the first 60 s after that for R0.
Record the enclosure temperature and humidity with every session. If you cannot keep them steady, the honest result is “uninformative”, not “no change”.
Re-baseline after a move, a repot, a season change, or a sensor swap.

docs.title: What the sensor is actually doing
body: Plants emit a mixture of biogenic volatile organic compounds. Wounding, ripening, and stress can change that mixture. A MOX array sees a combined, cross-sensitive response, not a single compound.
Metal-oxide sensors respond to humidity and temperature as well as to reducing gases. That is why the workspace refuses a change call when the enclosure moved.
There is no ethylene channel, so the app cannot make an ethylene claim. Do not use it to decide whether fruit will ripen.
Humidity, temperature, distance, and the room’s background air all affect the reading. Log them.

docs.title: What can go wrong
body: A change signal can be caused by watering, a draft, a new cleaning product, a person, or a different time of day. It is not specific to a pest or pathogen.
Pests and root problems can be present without a large VOC change. Inspect the plant.
A sensor that has drifted or been exposed to a strong VOC can report a change that is about the sensor, not the plant.
A dead or saturated channel is excluded from the change index. If every channel is dead, the workspace says so instead of reporting a quiet plant.

docs.title: The profile is a starting point, not evidence
body: The declared profile uses a 180 s warmup, a 60 s R0 window, a three-sample median, delta-over-R0 response, a two-channel corroboration floor, and a 90 s warning persistence with 25% hysteresis. Those values are reasoned defaults for a slow plant process on a small MOX array.

The host now enforces the corroboration floor, the confidence floor, and the coverage gate on the live path. That is a contract fix, not held-out evidence: these defaults have not been measured against a plant dataset.
The Vial therefore installs as Ungated and is not listed as reviewed evidence. If you collect a held-out report, add it to the evidence block. Do not describe these defaults as validated numbers.

home.headline: The plant is the evidence; the array is a change detector.
home.detail: The workspace compares the baseline-relative response to each channel’s own noise, withholds the call when the enclosure moved, and keeps a same-time-of-day session history.

metrics.label: Claim
metrics.hint: Same plant, same array, same time of day, and a steady enclosure.

metrics.label: Blind spot
metrics.hint: No ethylene channel; no ripening, pest, pathogen, or care-fault identification.

metrics.label: Best signal
metrics.hint: A change that holds for most of the window and repeats across sessions.

limits: No ethylene channel and no pest, pathogen, or care-fault identification.
Readings do not transfer across arrays, rooms, or seasons.
A change is a prompt to inspect, not a diagnosis; a quiet array does not clear visible symptoms.
